name: Daisy Duke
approach: Park at the Goats and Glaciers lookout on the Icefields Parkway south of Jasper townsite. The wall is visible from the road. Walk from the north end of the lot into the woods and push through deadfall and underbrush, aiming slightly right of the wall toward the talus field. Climb the talus, then head left up a steep small hill and follow scree and slab, staying right of the gully, up toward the base. Distinct roofs and a broken corner system facing right are the features that identify the line.
descent: Rappel the route, using the bolted stations and tree anchors. Partway down, a short walk toward climber's left along the treed ledge, past a gully and along a rock wall, leads to the next bolted station. The last rappels end at trees or the gully on
overview: Ten-pitch traditional quartzite route, mostly 5.6-5.7 and sustained, with plenty of good protection. One piton and no fixed anchors, so there is no easy bail. Pitch 4 (60 m) has the crux, a leftward traverse under a big roof; drag on the rope can be
path: Daisy Duke's Wall < Jasper National Park < Alberta < Canada

name: Bodhisatva
approach: Drive the Mount Edith Cavell road, which leaves the Icefields Parkway south of Jasper, to its end at the parking lot. Dune Wall is a conspicuous rock buttress at the foot of Mount Sorrow, to the right of Angel Glacier. Ford the creek and work up scree and stunted firs to the foot of the cliff. The route follows a left-facing corner reached past a ledge with a tree.
overview: Two pitches. The first passes a ledge with a tree and then follows the corner that faces left, ending at a chained belay. The second keeps going up that same corner and gets over a small roof.
path: Dune Wall < Jasper National Park < Alberta < Canada

name: Long Forgotten
approach: Drive the Mount Edith Cavell road, which leaves the Icefields Parkway south of Jasper, to its end at the parking lot. Dune Wall is a conspicuous rock buttress at the foot of Mount Sorrow, to the right of Angel Glacier. Ford the creek and work up scree and stunted firs to the foot of the cliff. The upper corner is the biggest corner system on the wall and is easily seen from the parking lot (a second large corner just to its left is not the route). Begin on the ramp that angles up and right towar
descent: Rappel the line back down its own anchors. The pitches are long, so check rope length against each station before you commit to the descent.
overview: Four or five pitches on good quartzite, with bolted anchors and variation options; protection is good except on pitch 1. P1 (5.5R, 55 m): obvious ramp rising right toward the primary corner system. P2 (5.6, 30 m): keep rising right to a two-bolt bela
path: Dune Wall < Jasper National Park < Alberta < Canada

name: Spiceworms
approach: Drive the Mount Edith Cavell road, which leaves the Icefields Parkway south of Jasper, to its end at the parking lot. Dune Wall is a conspicuous rock buttress at the foot of Mount Sorrow, to the right of Angel Glacier. Ford the creek and work up scree and stunted firs to the foot of the cliff. Spiceworms starts in the same spot as Stilgars Corner, and its anchors can be seen from the ground.
overview: A crack system trends up and left through dark rock to the base of an orange dihedral that faces left and is shallow. Place gear at a fixed angle and go up past flakes. When the corner gets steeper, step right (an old knifeblade is fixed here) into a
path: Dune Wall < Jasper National Park < Alberta < Canada

name: Stilgars Corner
approach: Drive the Mount Edith Cavell road, which leaves the Icefields Parkway south of Jasper, to its end at the parking lot. Dune Wall is a conspicuous rock buttress at the foot of Mount Sorrow, to the right of Angel Glacier. Ford the creek and work up scree and stunted firs to the foot of the cliff. Stilgars Corner is on the far right side of the wall and defines that sector.
descent: Rappel the route from its bolted belay stations, which carry rap rings, back to the base at the far right side of the Dune Wall.
overview: Stemming-rich corner. Pitch one carries the crux and is the finer of the pair; pitch two is easier yet still rewarding.
path: Dune Wall < Jasper National Park < Alberta < Canada

name: Unknown
approach: From the Edith Cavell road parking lot, cross the creek and scramble up scree and small trees to the base of the wall, the big rock buttress beside Angel Glacier's right edge. Walk along the base to the orange corner of Stilgar's Corner; this line starts just to its left, up a ledge reached by a scramble of low fifth class to the first bolt.
descent: Rappel from the two-bolt anchor on the grassy ledge. The bolts are old and rusty, so keep as little weight on them as you can.
overview: Poorly protected line near Stilgar's Corner; verify that the orange corner is that one, as a lesser corner lies next to this climb. Scramble at low fifth class to a small ledge and clip the bolt on the left (old horizontal hanger, rusted head). A lic
path: Dune Wall < Jasper National Park < Alberta < Canada

name: The Mammoth
approach: The Mendenhall Towers stand north of Juneau and can be reached by helicopter from town; the other ways are to ski north along Blackerby Ridge toward the glacier's northern fork, or to climb the glacier itself from the West Glacier trail. The glacier below The Curtain has the largest flat stretch beneath the towers and serves as the landing and camp spot for south-side routes, which need basic glacier travel skills. Looking from the Fourth Tower's south side, find the broad couloir descending; th
descent: Rappel the bolted rappel line down the route, keeping the ropes out of the cracks in the upper part.
overview: Climbs a crack system on an ear-shaped buttress of The Curtain, starting at the glacier and heading for the right side of a trunk-like feature. Seven pitches: P1 (5.10, 30m) under a roof, right, then back left on wide cracks and among pinnacles to a
path: 3rd/4th The Curtain < Mendenhall Towers < Juneau < Southeastern Alaska/Coastal Range

name: All That for a Hand Crack?
approach: The 5390 massif sits in the middle of Baranof Island east of Sitka and is remote. One approach begins where the gate blocks Sawmill Creek Road, and continues by bike or on foot to an old gravel pit beyond the hatchery, then follows flagging to the southern flank of Cross Mountain and links a chain of ridges to the massif; allow a full day. A shorter approach rides the road to Green Lake, crosses the lake by kayak, and climbs flagged ground to the ridge and across the alpine. Parties camp on the
descent: After the second pitch, mantel above the anchor onto the snow, which leads to the descent line. Walk off to the south over the snow, the same way as for the other routes on the west face.
path: 5390 West Face < 5390 Massif < Sitka < Southeastern Alaska/Coastal Range

name: Granitic Dreams

One approach begins where the gate blocks Sawmill Creek Road, and continues by bike or on foot to an old gravel pit beyond the hatchery, then follows flagging to the southern flank of Cross Mountain and links a chain of ridges to the massif; allow a full day. A shorter approach rides the road to Green Lake, crosses the lake by kayak, and climbs flagged ground to the ridge and across the alpine. Parties camp on the
descent: From the second anchor it is a short step to the top of the formation. Walk off to the south over the snow, the same way as the other west face routes. Rappelling this line is a poor idea because it is long, and snowmelt over the season lengthens it
overview: A dihedral on the West Face that shows as a dark ribbon in white granite. Length varies with snowpack: about 230 feet in June, with the first anchors near 140 feet, and at least 30-40 feet longer after summer melt. Begin in a corner of loose rock und
path: 5390 West Face < 5390 Massif < Sitka < Southeastern Alaska/Coastal Range

name: Crown Royal
approach: Little Switzerland on the Pika Glacier is reached by air taxi from Talkeetna. From the landing strip, ski or snowshoe up the glacier to Crown Jewel, the wide formation beside the Munchkin and the Royal Tower. The route begins from the saddle between Crown Jewel and the Royal Tower, between the Pika and Crown glaciers, on the Crown Jewel flank, at a buttress with a large hanging glacier on its west side. Cross the bergschrund and angle up and right on steepening snow to the rock below a big right
descent: Rappel the route rather than downclimbing the snow and crossing the bergschrund again at its foot. Long ropes make the descent easier.
overview: Start from the col separating Crown Jewel and Royal Tower, below a buttress with a large hanging glacier on its west flank. P1 crosses the bergschrund and angles up and right on steepening snow for about 200 ft to rock beneath a very large corner, wi
path: Crown Jewel < Little Switzerland < Denali National Park < Interior Alaska/Alaska Range

name: South Pillar - Free
approach: Devil's Thumb is reached by helicopter from Petersburg or by boat and foot from the coast. This route is on the south side. The approach comes up from the Cauldron beneath it, following a ramp system in the rock beside the southern icefall's west edge, a spot that suits a helicopter drop. A second way is to descend from the upper base camp, which passes under some objective hazard. Either way, cross the upper pocket glacier to the lower-angle rock ridge that leads to the south pillar, mostly thi
descent: Descend by rappelling the line you climbed. Below the traverse the rappels go down the open face until you re-enter the large corner system.
overview: Free variation of the south pillar, about 10 pitches; the breakdown is approximate because much was simul-climbed. P1 (5.8) starts at the notch, trends right past the roof, then back left. P2 (5.10) goes up and left to the lengthy corner system left
path: Devil's Thumb < Stikine Ice Cap < Southeastern Alaska/Coastal Range < Alaska

name: Shit in the Eye
approach: Lion's Head is a big igneous intrusion overlooking the Matanuska Glacier, reached from a pullout off the Glenn Highway near the communications tower. From the pullout take the trail, and cut right where it steepens. Sidehill around to the talus and descend along the cliff edge. The route climbs the west-facing cliff above Coyote Creek and starts below a clean face, taking the left line of the two weaknesses.
overview: A runout, sustained 5.7 first pitch trends up and left of a clean face and ends at a roof beneath a chossy corner. The next pitch climbs part of that corner, and the corner continues over more choss to a belay. Higher pitches alternate between ledgy,
path: Lion's Head < Mat-Su Valley Bouldering and Rock < Anchorage & South Central Alaska < Alaska

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: The Trolls are summits just south of the Throne in Little Switzerland, in Denali National Park, reached by air taxi from Talkeetna. Approach North Troll via the glacier from the landing strip. The route follows the northeast ridge and then the north face.
path: North Troll < Little Switzerland < Denali National Park < Interior Alaska/Alaska Range

name: NW Ridge Quadrant with Rabbit Ears Arete (s)
approach: From the Fairy Meadow hut, head up toward the lower Echo Glacier and pass below the small lakes on it to reach the notch on the northwest ridge of Quadrant. Dropping a little onto the east side of the ridge leads past the Rabbit Ears.
path: North Faces (from Fairy Meadow) < The Adamants < Selkirks (Northern) < British Columbia

name: Sentenel Peak - Shoofly Arete of North Ridge
approach: From the Fairy Meadow hut, hike as if going to Friendship Col, then branch right toward the ridge. The line begins on the lowest reaches of the Shoestring Glacier, almost opposite Quadrant's south face, and gains the northern end of Sentinel's north ridge.
overview: Starts on the lower Shoestring glacier and heads for the Sentinelle, the peak capping the north end of the North Ridge, with its pair of gunsite notches. Get onto the ridge and stay on its crest almost the whole way. Length and pitch counts are appro
path: North Faces (from Fairy Meadow) < The Adamants < Selkirks (Northern) < British Columbia

name: East Peak of Gothics - "North East" Ridge
approach: From the Fairy Meadow base camp take the usual path through Friendship Col onto the glacier. Bear right past Sentinel's south ridge, to the col between East Peak and Pioneer, then climb the steep snow slope up the north-northeast ridge to the first prominent rock step.
overview: From Fairy Meadow go through Friendship Col onto the Gothics Glacier, bear right past Sentinel's south ridge to the col between East Peak and Pioneer, then ascend the steep (usually) snow along the ridge running north-northeast until a conspicuous st
path: Gothics Neve Routes (via Friendship Col) < The Adamants < Selkirks (Northern) < British Columbia

name: Gibraltar North Face
approach: Gibraltar rises along the glacier's southern margin. From the Fairy Meadow base camp take the usual path through Friendship Col onto the glacier. The route starts at the obvious splitter hand crack, reached by stepping across the moat from a snow bank; check the moat edge before stepping, since the snow there can be undercut.
descent: Rappel the route. A long double-rope rappel from just below the mantle corner can reach the first pitch station, or it can be broken into shorter rappels.
overview: Four pitches. Pitch 1 is a splitter crack of roughly 35 m, from good hands (#2) narrowing to thin hands, then a brief fingers section at the top, 5.9 and arguably 10a up high, sustained with a couple of rests. P2 trends leftward on flakes and ledges,
path: Gothics Neve Routes (via Friendship Col) < The Adamants < Selkirks (Northern) < British Columbia

name: Divine Intervention
approach: The east face is reached by the Crescent Glacier. From the Kain hut, walk toward the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col but leave that route short of the col, exactly as for Crescent Spire; from the Applebee campground, hike north onto the moraine and follow the same line. The face is obvious from there. On that face, the line follows the central one of the three big corner systems that face left.
overview: A steep face climb up a dihedral line that is seldom repeated. Expect long stretches of 5.10 fingers and a few harder cruxes, the main one around pitch 5, where long reaches cross a face section as the dihedral fades; the crux pitch has face climbing
path: Bugaboo Spire < Purcell Mountains < British Columbia < Canada

name: Kain Route (South Ridge)
approach: From the Kain hut or the Applebee campground, follow the north lateral moraine of the Bugaboo Glacier, then cross the snowfield up to the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col. The climb follows the south arete from the col, starting with a long stretch of easy scrambling on ledges; carry an ice axe and possibly crampons for the snow below the col.
descent: Descend by the route itself, using rappels and scrambling. A rappel station sits at the Great Gendarme, and below the roped section the ridge is a scramble back down to the col.
overview: The south ridge of Bugaboo Spire, approached via moraine and snowfield to the col with Snowpatch, then along the south arete. Easy ledges for over 500' lead to a steep chimney, the point to rope up; it takes 120' in two strenuous leads to the ridge c
path: Bugaboo Spire < Purcell Mountains < British Columbia < Canada

name: Seppuku
approach: Follow the Sky Pilot approach to the Stadium Glacier and traverse west toward Copilot. Seppuku is on the north side of the peak, to the right of the main chimney that splits the face on the viewer's left; the first pitch climbs a right-arcing crack and slot that begins with a small roof.
descent: Rappel the NE route from bolted anchors.
overview: Harder than the standard Co-Pilot routes, with good rock and gear at the cruxes but plenty of moss and loose stone; a moderate alpine day trip from Squamish. Pitch 1 (50 m, 5.10b/c): begin on the slab beside the face-splitting gash, cross it with har
path: Copilot < Squamish < British Columbia < Canada

name: West Ridge
approach: Follow the normal Sky Pilot approach up to the Stadium Glacier, then cross easy snow slopes west to the foot of Copilot. Leave the snow and scramble up to the start of a corner, which is where the climbing begins; the scree can be extensive late in summer.
descent: Rappel the NE gully route.
overview: Three short pitches. First, 30 m at 5.5 straight up a corner to a ridge top. Second, 20 m climbing a few metres of low 5th to a broad ledge, then right and around to the peak's back side. Third, 15 m at 5.5 up a corner with some hand-crack moves to t
path: Copilot < Squamish < British Columbia < Canada

name: Energy Crisis
approach: From the Applebee campground, take the trail that leaves the east side of camp and climbs north onto the moraine. Pass the first lake on its west side and the second on its east side, then continue straight north up the Crescent Glacier to the south face of the spire. Parties staying at the Kain hut instead head toward the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col and turn right before reaching it to join the same glacier. The crack is just left of McTech Arete.
overview: Finger-sized splitter crack, then a layback up a corner.
path: Crescent Spire < Bugaboos < Columbia-Shushwap < British Columbia

Parties staying at the Kain hut instead head toward the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col and turn right before reaching it to join the same glacier. path: Crescent Spire < Bugaboos < Columbia-Shushwap < British Columbia

Pass the first lake on its west side and the second on its east side, then continue straight north up the Crescent Glacier to the south face of the spire. Parties staying at the Kain hut instead head toward the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col and turn right before reaching it to join the same glacier. name: Surprisingly Subsevere

name: Dehydrated on Dalwhinnie
approach: From the hut, cross the Dione Glacier to the foot of the south face. The route is on the southwest side of the peak, and the first two pitches can be skipped by using the SW spur from the Dione couloir.
overview: An alpine sport route whose rock is loose and whose route finding calls for trad habits. The recommended plan is to skip the opening pair of pitches and approach by the SW spur out of the Dione Couloir, the classic way in.
path: Dione < Tantalus Range < Sea to Sky (Squamish to Whistler) < British Columbia

name: Drilling Dionysus
approach: From the hut, cross the Dione Glacier to the base of the peak. The route is on the west side of Dione.
path: Dione < Tantalus Range < Sea to Sky (Squamish to Whistler) < British Columbia

name: SW Spur
approach: From the hut, cross the Dione Glacier to the foot of the south face. The route begins from the Dione couloir, where an easy fourth class ramp leads onto the rock on the southwest side of the peak.
overview: From the Dione couloir, an easy ramp at 4th class leads onto the rock. Cross into the couloir/face and look for the easiest line up. Several variations exist, with tricky protection and belays in places.
path: Dione < Tantalus Range < Sea to Sky (Squamish to Whistler) < British Columbia

name: The Howler
approach: Drive the Bannock forest road toward Gimli. From the Gimli base camp, head east toward a small peak, aim for the horizontal ridgeline running south from it, and cross over by way of a talus gully into the basin below Wolfs Ears. From the foot of the west ear, traverse east to the deep gully between the two ears. A shallow cave to the right of the gully marks the start of the first pitch.
descent: Rappel the route on single ropes back to its base. Some rappels use nearly a full rope, so knot the rope ends, and on the fifth pitch rappel on the outside of the chockstone.
path: East Ear < Wolfs Ears < Valhalla Mountains < Slocan Valley

name: Backpacker
approach: Park for the Hermit Meadows trail and hike to the end-of-trail sign, then continue a few minutes on a faint path to Hermit Bluff, the cracked outcrop on the left. Backpacker is in the middle of the crag, a hand crack leading to a blocky corner.
overview: A hand-sized crack leads into a blocky corner, and the route then continues up through a tree.
path: Hermit Bluff < Hermit Meadows Cragging < Rogers Pass < Columbia-Shushwap

name: Ionia NE Spur
approach: Approach through the Tantalus Range to the Lycia and Serratus col, and cross it to the Ionia Glacier. Cross the ice to the foot of the Ionia buttress, at its far right edge where the snow meets rock. The route climbs the northeast side of the peak from there.
overview: Mixed scrambling and roped climbing up the northeast side. Some pitches are on very loose rock; others have fine cracks and quartzite features. Higher pitches are more interesting, lower ones closer to scrambling, and the pitch count is flexible. Sta
path: Ionia Mountain < Tantalus Range < Sea to Sky (Squamish to Whistler) < British Columbia

name: West Ridge
approach: The usual approach goes up Nesakwatch Creek: a rough, high-clearance forest road leads to a trailhead, followed by a short, steep and strenuous trail to the base of the climb. The ridge is mainly scrambling with a few fifth-class sections, and no glacier travel is needed.
descent: The Northeast Ridge is used to descend. It alternates between snow and rock, with krummholz to push through and a few short rappels, and it ends in a basin on the Centre Creek side, well away from the Nesakwatch approach.
overview: A couple of fourth class moves on the ridge are followed by a pair of short pitches that reach a false summit. From there, round the corner on the left (exposed) and finish with a single chimney pitch. Descend with three rappels, each short enough fo
path: Mount Rexford < Western Chilliwack Range < Fraser Valley < British Columbia

name: Nesakwatch Enchainment (D)
approach: The spires are reached from the Nesakwatch Creek forest road, whose washouts and slides change from year to year, so check current access before driving. From where you park, walk the road past the washouts to the trail, which is easy to miss. It climbs steeply through forest and an old cutblock to a large granite wall, then bears right and up onto granite slabs and into the basin, where boulders make good bivouacs. The traverse begins on the north ridge of the North Spire.
descent: The traverse finishes on Rexford. Descend its west ridge, easy ridge walking on heather and granite blocks, following cairns to a gully; this is snow-filled early in the season, and it leads down between the South Spire and Rexford to the basin.
overview: A traverse over three summits: both Spires plus Rexford. Each Spire is climbed by its north ridge, then descended on the south side into the slim col beside Rexford. A few pitches on Rexford's brief NW face reach its top, and a walk down its west rid
path: Nesakwatch Spires < Western Chilliwack Range < Fraser Valley < British Columbia

name: Fingerberry Jam
approach: The Pigeon Feathers are the shorter spires above the East Creek basin, reached from Applebee Dome or the Kain Hut. The route is on the south face of West Peak, where obvious face-crack systems show from below. Start on a snow slope at a short dyke that leads to the left-arching finger crack.
descent: The last pitch is fourth-class scrambling over loose blocks to the top of the tower. The belay anchors are bolted, so descend by rappelling the route. Some of the rappels are long enough that a tag line is needed.
overview: Thin cracks, sharp to flared, joined by a brief traverse across the face. Begin on a snow slope below a left-arching fingercrack. P1 (5.11) climbs a wet dyke to a left-slanting fingercrack. P2 (5.11+) passes a roof into a stemming box. P3 (5.12-) use
path: Pigeon Feathers < Bugaboos < Columbia-Shushwap < British Columbia

name: Draco
approach: Reach the south face by taking the Bugaboo Glacier west, passing below the south face of Snowpatch Spire. The route starts from the midway glacial bench a short way above the toe of the face, where two large west-facing corners stand side by side. Begin in the center of the right wall of the westernmost corner, just right of a prominent arch, on the right-most crack that gains the ridge soonest.
descent: From the top, scramble down the east ridge until a ledge system on the south side leads back to the last bolted belay. Every belay on the route is bolted for rappelling, so parties descend by rappelling the line. A long rappel from the top of the fi
path: Pigeon Spire < Bugaboos < Columbia-Shushwap < British Columbia

name: Darn Gendarme
approach: The spire stands in Blackcomb Resort. Start at the Rendezvous Hut where the Blackcomb gondola ends, and pass the 7th Heaven chair and cross to the Horstman Glacier. From the upper end of the Showcase T-bar, turn north and follow the ridge crest; soon the spire appears straight ahead.
descent: The way off the spire is either an airy Tyrolean traverse across the chasm back to the ridge, or a more conventional rappel.
overview: The easiest line up this spire. Begin from a boulder and enter the clear crack that leans right; a few steep moves with good holds top out on an easy slab that carries one bolt. Cross the slab, swing round the arete on its left, and juggy holds lead
path: Showcase Spire < Sea to Sky (Squamish to Whistler) < British Columbia < Canada

name: East Ridge
approach: The route begins from Cairn Cabin by climbing the glacier to the Footstool, the feature at the foot of the steep east ridge. Access to the Sir Sandford group is long, with several sub-ranges between it and the Rogers Pass area.
overview: Very steep ridge, rated R, of decomposed marble whose granulation resembles BBs or corn snow; a boot, glove or axe adze rubbed on it produces a hold. The first-ascent party needed approximately 16 hours, starting from the high camp by the Footstool.
path: Sir Sanford Group < Selkirks (Northern) < British Columbia < Canada

name: Furry Pink Arete
approach: Start at the end of the park road at the Bugaboo Creek trailhead and take the Conrad Kain Hut trail, about 5 km one way with roughly 700 m of gain, steep and with chained sections near the top. Climbers camp at the hut or at the Applebee Dome campground on the rock slab above it. The route lies just south of the Kraus-McCarthy rappel line on the west face, which makes it a short outing from the col. The west face is reached by crossing the glacier to the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col; rope up for crevas
descent: The route tops out beside the Kraus-McCarthy rappel line, so the rappel stations are right there. Rappel that line on its bolted and chained anchors and finish via the Bugaboo-Snowpatch col or the Pigeon-Snowpatch rappels.
overview: The start is somewhat scruffy, but the climbing cleans up higher. Pitch 7 is a classic crux.

name: Sendero Norte
approach: Start at the end of the park road at the Bugaboo Creek trailhead and take the Conrad Kain Hut trail, about 5 km one way with roughly 700 m of gain, steep and with chained sections near the top. Climbers camp at the hut or at the Applebee Dome campground on the rock slab above it. The route climbs the centre of the east face: descend to the glacier below the wall and walk to the base, stepping across the moat at the rock, which gets harder as summer goes on. Bring an axe and rope for the glacier.

name: Tantalus Standard Route
approach: The route is reached by crossing the Dione Glacier below the peak. Expect a bergschrund at the base of the climb, where a screw or a picket helps.
descent: Descend by reversing the line of ascent.
